newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain to report to EU on progress in BSE battle.
newsitem.headline: Britain to report to EU on progress in BSE battle.

text.p: Britain is expected to inform European Union farm ministers on Monday of progress in the fight against mad cow disease but will not press for an easing of a worldwide ban on its beef exports.
EU officials said Britain would not seek at the meeting to exempt herds certified to be free of the deadly disease Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).

Exemption of these grass-fed herds, primarily in Northern Ireland, would be a first step in easing the ban imposed by the EU in March after Britain disclosed a possible link between BSE and its fatal human equivalent Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
"The British government will just report on the state of play on measures to combat and monitor the disease," an Irish EU Presidency official said.

Irish farm minister Ivan Yates said last month after the EU agreed a BSE beef aid package that a majority of member states were sympathetic to a certified herd scheme in Northern Ireland, where there is a computerised system for tracing animals.
But he stressed it was up to London to make a move.

British officials said the government was waiting for the advice of EU veterinary scientists on whether a selective cull of up to 147,000 extra cattle was necessary after a British study claimed the disease could die out within five years.

The cull, which would supplement the annual slaughter of one million older animals over the age of 30 months, was part of a deal struck by EU leaders in Florence in June to defuse the mad cow crisis and restore consumer confidence.

Under the deal Britain agreed to tighten controls to ensure that animal feed did not contain infected meat and bone meal, widely believed to be the cause of the epidemic. Slaughter house inspections and cattle identification are also being improved.
Nearly 900,000 older animals have been killed and the backlog in the programme should be cleared by the end of 1996, British officials said.
This would allow the government, depending on the scientific advice and parliament's approval, to implement the extra cull.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, backed by member states, has insisted that Britain carry out the extra cull before any easing of the crippling ban.

The European Commission, which is fending off growing allegations of mishandling the BSE crisis made at a European Parliament committee of inquiry, is anxious to be seen as following scientific advice.

On Friday, a spokesman denied that a decision on June 11 to lift the embargo on British gelatine -- a beef by-product widely used in food, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals -- was intended to facilitate a compromise at the Florence summit.
"That's rubbish," agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said, stressing the decision was based on available scientific evidence and subject to strict conditions.
Several experts told the committee that the gelatine decision was premature and that further research was needed.
British gelatine exports had not yet resumed and any request would be refused until the new research was ready, Kiely said.
